titleStmt.title: Letter from John Chamberlain to Dudley Carleton, 7 November 1605

publicationStmt.p: Published digitally at earlymodernletters.org. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

div.p: Though I looked for you before this time, and have often wisht you here among your old schoolefellowes that are almost all come up to the Parliament: yet as matters are lately fallen out about your Lord,Henry Percy (1564–1632), ninth Earl of Northumberland — Carleton's former employer, in whose household Carleton had served as a secretary. His kinsman Thomas Percy was one of the principal Gunpowder Plot conspirators, which cast instant suspicion on the Earl despite his own probable innocence. He was examined by the Privy Council, committed to the Tower, and eventually fined £30,000 and stripped of his offices — a punishment driven as much by factional politics as by evidence. Chamberlain is glad Carleton is away from the fallout. am well content you be absent. Not that your Lord (as I hope) can be any way toucht with this divelish conspiracie in bloude, but that neerenes of name, longe and inward dependance, and familiaritie, cannot but leave some aspersion, that will not easilie or lightly be washt of without time: in which consideration I heare he is rather wisht then willed to kepe his house.

I cannot but remember what you have divers times told me touching Thomas Percie,Thomas Percy (c. 1560–1605), great-grandson of Henry Percy, fourth Earl of Northumberland, and agent of the ninth Earl in the North. He was one of the five original conspirators of the Gunpowder Plot, having rented the vault beneath the House of Lords in the name of "Thomas Percy." He fled London on the night of 4–5 November and was killed resisting arrest at Holbeche House, Staffordshire, on 8 November 1605 — the day after this letter was written. that you suspected him to be a subtile flattering daungerous knave. He hath not only verefied your judgement, but exceeded all degrees of comparison, and gon beyond Nero and Caligula that wisht all Rome but one head that they might cut yt of at a stroke, for he at one blowe wold have ruined the whole realme.

He had hired the house or lodging next to the Parliament, together with the seller or vault under the upper house:The vault or undercroft beneath the House of Lords, running beneath the building along the river side of the Old Palace of Westminster. Percy rented it in the name of a coal and wood merchant — a cover that explained the presence of barrels and billets. The undercroft was adjacent to the Chamber of the Lords where the King would deliver his speech at the State Opening on 5 November 1605. into which by the meanes of one JohnsonThe name given by Guy Fawkes (1570–1606) when he was arrested. Fawkes maintained the alias "John Johnson" for several days under examination before his true identity was established. He had spent months as the undercroft's keeper, loading it with powder under cover of the coal and wood merchant's lease. his man (a superstitious papist, or rather a priest as is thought) he hath this twelvemoneth as any time conveyed as much pouder in sachells, and firkins could contein, fowre or five and thirty barrells, hoggesheads,Thirty-five barrels of gunpowder — enough, experts calculated, to have destroyed not only the Parliament building but every structure within a wide radius. Contemporary accounts marvelled at the scale of the stockpile. Chamberlain's "sachells and firkins" accurately reflects the variety of containers used: small sacks, small casks, and large barrels, packed around iron bars and stones to increase the shrapnel effect. with intent the first day of the parlement when the King shold be in his speach to blowe them all up: and had so cunningly covered them with billets, faggots and such trash, that without long search they could not be discovered, and but that God blinded him or some of his, to send this inclosed without name or date to the Lord Mountegle,William Parker (1575–1622), fourth Baron Monteagle and son-in-law of the conspirator Thomas Tresham. On the evening of 26 October 1605 he received an anonymous letter warning him not to attend the Parliament ("for though there be no appearance of any stir, yet I say they shall receive a terrible blow this Parliament"). He brought it immediately to Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury, who showed it to the King. The letter's authorship has never been definitively established; Francis Tresham, Monteagle's brother-in-law, is the most common suspect. yt was very like to take effect.

But the carieng yt to the Lord of SalisberieRobert Cecil (1563–1612), first Earl of Salisbury; Principal Secretary of State and, from 1608, Lord Treasurer. He received the Monteagle letter and, after showing it to the King, organized the search of the vaults. His management of the Plot's discovery and aftermath cemented his position as the dominant minister of the early Jacobean government. and so to the King, yt gave such light, that watch being set, the fellowe was taken making his traines"Traines" = the fuses or trains of powder laid to lead the fire to the main charge; the technical vocabulary of artillery and mining. Guy Fawkes was caught in the act of preparing to ignite the powder. at midnight with a blinde lanterne,A dark lantern — a lantern with a shutter or slide that could conceal the flame while still providing light to the bearer. It was a device associated with clandestine operations; its discovery on Fawkes became one of the iconic images of the Plot. and presently confessed the plot, yet with such shew of resolution that he seemed to be cheifly greved that yt had wanted successe. The next day caried to the Towre, but what Sir William WaadeSir William Wade (also Waad, c. 1546–1623), Lieutenant of the Tower of London from 1605 to 1613. As Lieutenant he was responsible for the examination of prisoners; under his watch Fawkes was tortured on the rack until he gave up the names of his co-conspirators and signed a confession in a visibly shaking hand. (that is lieutenant) and other examiners have wrange out of him I cannot learne: only I heare Sir Edward BainhamSir Edward Baynham (d. 1618), a Catholic recusant and soldier who had served in the Irish wars. He had been in Rome carrying a message about the Plot to the English Jesuit superior Robert Persons — making him a conspirator in the wider circle around the Plot even if not one of the vault-men. He was indeed captured, examined, and eventually acquitted for lack of direct evidence. he was come lately out of the Lowe Countries is sought for: and some five or sixe Jesuites and priests taken in a privie search. Percie comming up on a sleveles errand"Sleveles" = pointless, fruitless — from "sleeveless," having no obvious purpose. Percy had come to London supposedly to report to the ninth Earl of Northumberland on northern affairs; Chamberlain's aside implies that the real purpose was to check on the Plot's readiness. and before he was looked for to your Lord, durst not tarry to see the event, but went away that night that his man was taken.

Curious folkes observe that this deliveraunce hapned to the King the fift of AugustThe Gowrie Conspiracy of 5 August 1600, in which James VI of Scotland was allegedly lured into a trap by the Gowrie brothers at Perth. James escaped and the brothers were killed. The coincidence of dates — both 5 August and 5 November fell on a Tuesday in their respective years — struck contemporaries as providential, confirming James's divine protection. aunswerable to the fift of November, both Tewsdayes, and this plot to be executed that at Johnstowne.Perth (or Gowrie House in Perth), the scene of the 1600 Gowrie attempt, was sometimes called "Johnstown" in Scots usage.
On Tewsday at night we had great ringing and as great store of bonfires as ever I thincke was seene. And this is all I can write or remember in this matter.

The Earle of CumberlandGeorge Clifford (1558–1605), third Earl of Cumberland; naval commander and privateer, famous for his voyages against Spanish Caribbean ports. He died on 30 October 1605, leaving the earldom to his brother Francis (who became the fourth Earl). His daughter Anne (Lady Anne Clifford, 1590–1676) received £15,000–16,000 on condition she make no further claim to the estate — a settlement she contested for decades, becoming famous for her determined pursuit of her inheritance rights. died of a flixeFlux (dysentery). A common early modern cause of death, particularly for soldiers and sailors whose campaigns exposed them to contaminated water and crowded, unsanitary conditions. the 3oth of October leaving the earledome to his brother, and fifteen or sixten thousand pound to his daughter, so she make no further claime; his Lady and he were reconciled not longe before his death, but yt fell out odly that he desiring she shold receve consecrated with him she was not prepared.

The Lord KnollesWilliam Knollys (1547–1632), first Earl of Banbury; Comptroller and then Treasurer of the Household under James I. His wife Dorothy was the widow of William Brydges, fourth Baron Chandos, hence "the old Lady Chandos." Knollys subsequently and infamously married a woman forty years his junior, Elizabeth Howard, who bore children later claimed to be by other fathers. is newly become a widower by the death of his old Lady Chandos.

Dr. AndrewesLancelot Andrewes (1555–1626), scholar-bishop and one of the great preachers of the age; chief editor of the Authorized Version of the Bible (1611). His consecration as Bishop of Chichester on 3 November 1605 — two days before the Gunpowder Plot was discovered — positioned him for a long ecclesiastical career under James I (he was later translated to Ely and then Winchester). was consecrated bishop of Chichester on Sonday last: the manages of the earle of EssexRobert Devereux (1591–1646), third Earl of Essex; son of the executed second Earl. He was to marry Frances Howard, daughter of Thomas Howard, Earl of Suffolk; the match, arranged when both were children, ultimately proved catastrophic — Frances later sought an annulment, claiming non-consummation, in one of the great scandals of the Jacobean court. and the younge Lord CrambourneWilliam Cecil (1591–1668), Viscount Cranborne; son of Robert Cecil, Earl of Salisbury. He was to marry Catherine Howard, sister of Frances — the double match linking the Cecil and Howard families. He later became the second Earl of Salisbury. to the Lord ChamberlainesThomas Howard (1561–1626), first Earl of Suffolk; Lord Chamberlain of England 1603–14. His two daughters Frances and Catherine were the brides in these arranged matches, contracted when the children were very young. The double ceremony eventually took place in January 1606. daughters are put of till toward Christmas.

Sir Edwin SandsSir Edwin Sandys (1561–1629), parliamentarian and colonial promoter; later a leading figure in the Virginia Company. His Europae Speculum, an account of the state of religion across Europe, was published in 1605 without his consent under the title A Relation of the State of Religion. Sandys himself appears to have arranged its condemnation by the High Commission to suppress unauthorized copies — an early example of an author using ecclesiastical authority to manage their own text. bookes were burnt on Satterday in Paules Churchyard by order of the high commission and not without his owne consent as is saide.

Fraunces BaconFrancis Bacon (1561–1626), philosopher, lawyer, and statesman. The Two Bookes of Francis Bacon. Of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, Divine and Humane (1605) — dedicated to James I — was one of the founding documents of empirical philosophy, arguing for the systematic reform of knowledge through observation and experiment. Its publication in the same week as the Gunpowder Plot is one of the small ironies of early modern intellectual history. hath set foorth a new worke of the proficience and advancement of learning.

Monsieur Beaumont Christophe de Harlay (c. 1557–1629), Comte de Beaumont, French ambassador to England from 1602 to 1605. He had been a capable diplomatist but his departure was marred by an unseemly scramble for gifts and perquisites. Chamberlain's "mecanicall tricks" means low, base, mercenary behaviour — the conduct of a tradesman rather than a courtier. "To robbe the Egiptians" is a biblical allusion to Exodus 12, where the Israelites, on departing Egypt, asked for and received gold and silver from their neighbours — a kind of legalised plunder. Chamberlain applies it here with characteristic irony. the French ambassador went homeward the first of this moneth, and hath blotted his former reputation with very mecanicall tricks at parting: for having 2000 ounces of plate geven him he cavilled for 500 more, as having seene a president of the like, which being graunted him, he begd two horses more by name of the King, besides pictures great and small with jewells at his owne appointment, and not a noble man or other of his neere acquaintaunce but he got horses, geldings or somwhat of him: and the impost of 60 tunne of wine of the Lord Treasurer which he sold to French marchants for threescore pound: with divers other such petti larceries, as yf he made no conscience to robbe the Egiptians.

We heare that Master Winwod hath a sonne, and that the States and the Lady Conway were his gossipps.Gossips here = godparents. Ralph Winwood's eldest son Richard was born in the Netherlands in late 1605, where Winwood was serving as English agent to the States-General. The "States" (the States-General of the Dutch Republic) and Lady Conway (Dorothy, wife of Sir Edward Conway, who was also active in the Netherlands) standing as godparents reflects the close social world of English diplomats and their Dutch hosts.
Thus praeing you to remember my satten and the other trincketts I commit you to God in great haste.

postscript.p: To my assured goode frend Master Dudley Carleton geve these at Paris.
